title: Premature In-Memory Sharding (Partitioning without Contention)
pattern: Splitting an in-memory collection or state store into a large array of locks (shards) before observing or profiling any thread lock contention.
why_bad: Sharding introduces significant architectural complexity, memory allocation overhead, and complicates global operations (like resizing, clearing, or listing elements) which must lock all shards sequentially, potentially causing deadlocks and worse performance [9, 12, 104].
detection: Using a vector or array of mutexes/read-write locks (`Vec<Mutex<T>>`) accessed via key hashing where a single lock over the collection is sufficient for low-concurrency or single-threaded use.
counterexample: High-throughput systems (such as high-traffic web servers with 64+ cores) where lock profiling explicitly demonstrates that lock acquisition wait times exceed 20% of thread execution time. `Contextual`.
source: *1701.00854v6.pdf*, Chapter 6, Section 6.4 (p. 12); *Thinking in Systems*, Section 3.2 (p. 104); *Database Internals*, Chapter 1.
